slides.headline: These ants sew with their own babies.
slides.sub: How weaver ants stitch living leaves into a home

slides.headline: Step 1: pull the leaves together
slides.body: Teams of workers grip a leaf edge in their jaws and curl it into place. Across gaps, they grab each other and use their own bodies as bridges.

slides.headline: Step 2: use a larva as a needle
slides.body: Workers carry nearly mature larvae to the seam and tap their heads. Each larva releases silk and is passed back and forth like a living shuttle.

slides.headline: Adults can't spin. Only larvae can.
slides.body: Silk comes only from larvae at the start of their final growth stage, so the colony's young supply the thread for every wall.

slides.label: workers in a mature colony, all from one queen
slides.body: Housed in hundreds of leaf nests across neighbouring trees. Outpost nests at the edges hold the oldest workers.

slides.headline: The oldest pest control on record
slides.body: Farmers in China have placed weaver ant nests in crop trees for at least 1,700 years. It is the oldest known use of insects as biological control.

slides.headline: Send this to someone who sews.
slides.body: One species, properly sourced, every week. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
Weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina) build their nests by sewing living leaves together with silk from their own larvae.

Workers hold the leaf edges in place while others carry a larva to the seam and pass it back and forth like a shuttle. Because they are not limited to existing tree holes, one colony can grow to about half a million workers spread over many trees, and the ants bite and spray formic acid to defend them.

Swipe for the full story. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Britannica (2025); Peeters & Andersen 1989, Psyche.
